claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.label: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
claims.statement: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.

operationalizations.text: Extract opposing parastichy families from calibrated sunflower images and measure their local intersection angles across each disc and among heads. Approximate constancy away from 90 degrees supports the claim; systematic angle variation or frequent orthogonality refutes it.

On annotated sunflower discs, measure the angle at which clockwise and anticlockwise parastichies meet at many radii. Isogonal intersection is confirmed if that angle is constant within heads and orthogonal crossing is uncommon across heads; a concentration of intersection angles at 90° would support Church's special case instead.

obstacles: Herbarium images may distort three-dimensional capitula.
Parastichy tracing can be ambiguous near the disc center and edge.
The open images are domesticated sunflower heads, not a sample of other capitula.
Disordered regions of some heads do not define a single intersection angle.

claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.label: Chondriosomes and similar fibrils are surface-tension clumps drawn along the cell axis
claims.statement: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force and dynamical polarity in the cell.

operationalizations.text: Test whether mitochondrial and fibrillar structures have stable molecular identities and functions and whether their axial distributions are better predicted by active transport and organelle biogenesis than by passive surface-tension clumping.

Ask whether mitochondria are bounded organelles with a characteristic proteome and functions, or unstructured clumps of mixed cytoplasm drawn to a cell pole. A double membrane, a mitochondrial proteome and a distributed network would refute the clump account; granules with no specific composition, gathered and drawn out with the cell axis, would support it.

obstacles: The claim combines several distinct structures and cell types.
Surface tension and osmotic currents are not directly measured in most archives.
The same resources do not cover every non-mitochondrial fibril the wording also includes.
Mammalian cultured cells dominate the image sets relative to germ cells and invertebrate tissues.

Subcellular images showing mitochondrial localization across human cell types named in the claim

roles: Inventory of mammalian mitochondrial proteins, sub-compartments and pathways, used to test whether these bodies have a specific identity

claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.label: Four cells of a segmenting egg never meet in a point; a polar furrow is always present
claims.statement: In the four-celled stage of a segmenting egg whose cells are in full fluid contact, the four cells cannot meet in a single point; a short intermediate partition (the polar furrow) must be present, and reports of four cells meeting in a simple cross are due to error or imperfect observation.

operationalizations.text: Reconstruct four-cell embryos in 3D and test whether any full-contact configuration has a four-way junction rather than an intervening polar furrow.

In four-cell embryos whose blastomeres are in full contact, score whether a polar furrow is present or the four cells meet at one point. A short intermediate partition in essentially every such embryo would support the claim; stable four-way crosses in fully apposed fluid blastomeres would refute it.

obstacles: The full-fluid-contact condition must be distinguished from partial adhesion.
Some species and imaging orientations are underrepresented.
A cross seen in a single optical plane can hide a short polar furrow, so only 3D or time-resolved volumes are decisive.
Molluscs and annelids, classical material for this stage, are less completely archived than frog and sea urchin.

roles: Open embryo time-lapse and volumetric microscopy across model animals.

roles: Sea-urchin developmental images and associated resources for early cleavage geometry

roles: Public multidimensional early-development imaging.

claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.label: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles
claims.statement: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.

operationalizations.text: Measure parent and daughter diameters and branch angles in segmented arterial trees, then regress angle on relative branch caliber and test symmetry for equal daughters. A flat or reversed relationship would refute the rule.

At each bifurcation, measure the branch angle and the daughter-to-parent radius ratio. The claim is supported if angle declines as relative branch size increases, with the smallest side branches near 70-90 degrees and equal daughters leaving at equal angles; a flat or reversed angle-size relation would refute it.

obstacles: Clinical scans favor large vessels.
Branch angle depends on organ, flow state and imaging posture.
Angles measured from projected angiograms differ from true three-dimensional angles.
Open trees sample humans heavily and leave most vertebrate groups unmeasured.

claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.label: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species
claims.statement: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.

operationalizations.text: Classify eight-cell partition topology in multiple embryos from the same species and test whether more than one essentially different arrangement occurs.

Classify the surface partition pattern of many eight-cell frog eggs and test whether more than one topological type occurs at appreciable frequency. Several recurring arrangements within the species would support the claim; a single arrangement in nearly every egg would refute it.

obstacles: Some datasets contain few embryos per species.
Equivalent 3D arrangements can look different in 2D projections.
Atlas images preferentially show a textbook arrangement, which is the sampling bias the claim is warning against.
A frequency count needs many individual eggs, and public atlases are not already tabulated that way.

claims.label: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites
claims.statement: In some ammonoids the spiral angle changes progressively during growth: where it increases the whorls become narrower (as in Oekotraustes), and where it diminishes towards zero the coil opens out into an almost straight curve (as in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites).

operationalizations.text: Measure local spiral angle and whorl breadth through ontogeny in the named ammonoids and test whether increasing angle predicts narrowing while decline toward zero predicts uncoiling. Alternative local curve models provide direct comparison.

Measure spiral angle through ontogeny in Oekotraustes, Scaphites, Ancyloceras, Lituites and similar shells. An increasing angle with narrowing whorls, and a decreasing angle toward an open hook, support the claim; constant angle despite those outlines, or the opposite angle trend, refutes it for those taxa.

obstacles: Fossil crushing can distort local angles.
Some named historical taxa have revised classifications.
3D scans of these particular genera are fewer than photographs, and crushed specimens distort the later whorls.
A change in outline can reflect translation or aperture shape as well as the spiral angle.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Open fossil shell scans preserve ontogenetic coiling trajectories.
CT of heteromorph ammonoids where deposited, for ontogenetic angle along the shell.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally
claims.statement: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.

operationalizations.text: Estimate species range sizes, occupancy, local richness, dominance and fossil first occurrences from georeferenced living and fossil records, with standardized sampling and taxonomic validation. The claim predicts unusually broad ranges, high local richness, weak dominance and long genus or family durations.

From occurrence tables, measure geographic range sizes, sample-level richness and evenness, and the stratigraphic span of families and genera, including whether living taxa are already present in the Cambrian. Cosmopolitan ranges, high local richness without single-species dominance, and Cambrian-to-Recent identity would support the claim; endemic ranges, dominance, or much later first appearances would refute the corresponding clause.

obstacles: Micropaleontological taxonomy has substantial synonymy and revision.
Sampling effort is highly uneven in space, depth and geological time.
Sampling effort and taxonomic lumping can mimic cosmopolitanism and high local richness.
Deep-sea drilling archives are strongest in the Cenozoic, so Paleozoic coverage depends on other occurrence compilations.

roles: Public georeferenced occurrence records for living marine Radiolaria.
Living marine occurrence records for testing whether radiolarian species lack geographic limits.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.label: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface
claims.statement: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.

operationalizations.text: Fit a single smooth spheroid or ellipsoid to the 3D branch centerlines and tine tips of paired antlers, comparing residuals with separate surfaces and unconstrained branching models. Consistently small residuals and bilateral continuity support the claim; strongly noncoplanar or multi-surface arrangements refute it.

Place landmarks on tine tips of paired antlers and fit a single ellipsoid or spheroid, allowing mirror symmetry across the midline. The claim is supported if one surface accounts for both antlers within a small residual and the tips lie on a continuous curve; systematically separate surfaces for left and right, or residuals that grow with tine length, would refute it.

obstacles: Damage and annual age affect tine completeness.
A tolerance for being 'confined' to one surface must be prespecified.
Many scans are of skulls after the antlers were shed, or of a single antler.
Open 3D coverage is good for a few deer species and poor for the rest of Cervidae.

claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.label: Human and anthropoid skulls show divergent rather than linear evolutionary change
claims.statement: No continuous transformation series passes through known fossil and living human and anthropoid skulls (Mesopithecus, Pithecanthropus, Neanderthal, modern man), indicating that there is no single straight line of descent and that their variation has been divergent.

operationalizations.text: Compare branching versus single-line models using genomic and morphological phylogenies of living and fossil hominids and apes. Robust non-ladder topology and incompatible transformation trajectories support divergent variation.

Ask whether one transformation series can be drawn through Mesopithecus, Homo erectus (Pithecanthropus), Neanderthals and modern humans with lower error than a branching arrangement of the same skulls. A large advantage for the branching model would support divergent change; a single series that passes through the fossils in order would refute it.

obstacles: Historical taxon names require modern mapping.
Fossil incompleteness affects exact branching order.
Key fossils are few, often reconstructed, and unevenly available for download.
Which specimens are admitted as successive stages changes whether a straight series appears to fail.

roles: Fossil and living primate cranial scans.

claims.label: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts
claims.statement: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.

operationalizations.text: Sample curves from simultaneously formed soft outlines and incrementally accreted hard parts, fit logarithmic and rival models, and test association between accretion mode, logarithmic fit and visible growth lines. Credible logarithmic soft-tissue counterexamples would refute the exclusion.

Fit logarithmic spirals to accretionary hard parts (shell, tusk, horn, claw) and to structures built all at once (leaf margins, fish outlines). Better unique fits, usually with growth lines, in the first class, and poor fits in the second, support the prediction.

obstacles: Determining whether a part is formed simultaneously may require developmental knowledge.
Curve fitting is sensitive to landmark and scale selection.
Some leaf margins and fin outlines can approximate a spiral over a short arc, so the test needs a pre-set fit criterion.
Claws and tusks are less densely archived than shells.

claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.label: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.

operationalizations.text: Test whether the abundance and size distribution of dead foraminiferal tests across marine sediment grain-size fractions correlate with hydraulic settling velocity equivalence (Shields parameter / settling speed matching host quartz grains) rather than living habitat avoidance.

Model foraminiferal shell abundance across sediment grain-size and current-speed gradients, including transport and settling traits, and compare hydraulic-sorting predictions with habitat-avoidance models based on living assemblages. Matching dead-shell distributions but different live distributions would support sorting; absence from both after flow controls would support avoidance.

Regress living and dead foraminiferal abundance on sediment grain size across surface samples, treating grain size as the current-speed proxy Thompson uses. Hydraulic sorting is supported if dead tests track the fine fraction the way other light particles do, including where living animals are present in coarser patches; habitat avoidance is favored if stained living specimens are absent from gravels even when transport is accounted for.

obstacles: Epiphytic or epilithic taxa attached to coarse substrates while alive may be winnowed away only after death.
Many assemblage datasets mix living and dead tests.
Dissolution and sampling gear also alter shell distributions.
Foraminiferal protocols often discard the coarse fraction, so true gravels are under-sampled.
Most open pairs of counts and grain size are regional shelves, estuaries, or single cores.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.label: Parastichy counts on fir-cones are nearly constant within a species
claims.statement: The numbers of conspicuous parastichies on fir-cones are on the whole very constant within a species, e.g. 5 and 3 in the Norway spruce and 8 and 5 in the common larch.

operationalizations.text: Count opposing parastichy families in many georeferenced cones per conifer species and estimate within-species frequency distributions, explicitly checking the stated 5/3 spruce and 8/5 larch modes. Tight species-specific modes support the claim; broad variation or different dominant counts refutes it.

Count the conspicuous parastichy pairs on many cones per species, including Norway spruce and larch, and partition the variance within and among species. Constancy is supported if one pair dominates each species, such as 5 and 3 in spruce and 8 and 5 in larch; frequent within-species switching among distant pairs would refute it.

obstacles: Images must show the cone at sufficient resolution and orientation.
Cultivar, age and cone position may contribute within-species variation.
Large published cone counts (pines, larches, spruces) are summarized in papers and are not one open raw file.
Cone size varies within species, which Thompson elsewhere expects to change the visible pair.
